Model it as a permanently installed or portable information, identification, advertising, route, menu, score, warning, or display asset with readable hierarchy and credible support. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Panel shape, scale, mounting, viewing angle, border or bezel, and support must identify the sign category before text is read. Lettering cannot be the sole distinction. Keep the working envelope near 1.2 meters wide, 0.16 meters deep, and 2.4 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Course Arrow Sign; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Model panel thickness, border, bezel, backing, posts or wall brackets, fasteners, electrical access, cable routing, weather protection, and foundations where applicable. Required visible components are shaped sign panel, border or reflective trim, modeled or changeable content layer, post, wall bracket, or portable support, rear backing, fasteners and mounting collars, foundation or wall connection, information panel or display surface, border or protective bezel, backing structure, post, bracket, frame, or portable base, fasteners and attachment hardware, lettering, symbols, or changeable content layer, power, lighting, or service access where required. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary engineered steel, sandstone, safety paint, weather-resistant hardware, rust, safety orange, steel, turquoise water, desert green. large-scale canyon adventure infrastructure; engineered platforms, bridges, rescue equipment, rock integration, believable supports and safety systems. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: floating shapes without supports, toy obstacle pieces, unreadable scale. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Mount it to the named wall, post, facade, roadside foundation, kiosk base, ceiling support, menu stand, scoreboard frame, or portable base at a deliberate viewing height and angle. Backing, supports, power, weather protection, and service access may not disappear into or float away from the mounting surface. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Keep lettering, logos, display surfaces, indicator lights, changeable panels, and emissive layers separate for localization, state changes, damage, content updates, and nighttime use. Expected hooks include changeable display, content, or emissive state, day, night, powered, warning, and damaged light states. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the primary viewing face and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground support, wall-mount center, hanging point, or portable base. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use mesh or texture lettering according to viewing distance. LODs must preserve panel shape, color block, mounting, primary wordmark, and display state without excessive geometry. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 14,040 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 6,480 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 2,160 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Panel shape, scale, mounting, viewing angle, border or bezel, and support must identify the sign category before text is read. Lettering cannot be the sole distinction.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Course Arrow Sign is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Keep the working envelope near 4 meters wide, 3 meters deep, and 3 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Course Zipline Handle; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Snap it to the road, path, bridge, dock, rail, platform, course, or terrain grid with exact edge continuity, matching elevation, consistent width, correct travel direction, believable support spacing, and continuous simplified collision. No gaps, overlaps, floating ends, or invisible ledges are allowed. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Define walk, drive, climb, jump, grind, checkpoint, hazard, fall, docking, and connection boundaries through named surfaces and sockets. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use continuous simplified traversal collision matching grades, gaps, curbs, rails, docking edges, fall boundaries, and platform surfaces. Decorative cracks, bolts, grates, trim, and surface noise must not create snagging micro-collision. Use positive Z as the travel or module-continuation direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the documented grid center, connection edge, spline point, or docking plane. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use modular dimensions, shared materials, and continuous simplified collision. Distant LODs may reduce cracks and hardware but cannot change grade, gaps, width, edge safety, or traversal timing. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 14,040 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 6,480 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 2,160 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Course Zipline Handle is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.
